questions.q: In Freytag's scheme for a five-act tragedy, where does the climax fall?
choices: In the middle of the play, around the third act
questions.explain: Freytag's climax is the high point at the center of the play; the fall and catastrophe follow.

questions.q: What does Freytag call the moment that sets the action going after the introduction?
questions.explain: The exciting force is Freytag's term. The others belong to Vogler, Egri and Propp.

questions.q: A tragedy's last act drags because the audience can see the ending coming. Which Freytag device addresses this?
choices: The force of final suspense, a last moment of hope before the catastrophe
questions.explain: Freytag knew the fall is hard to sustain and valued a late moment of uncertainty to renew suspense.

questions.q: Which sequence matches Freytag's five parts?
choices: Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, denouement
Introduction, rise, climax, return or fall, catastrophe
Inciting incident, complications, crisis, climax, resolution
questions.explain: The first is the simplified school version; the last is McKee's five-part design.

questions.q: What starts the downward movement just after Freytag's climax?
questions.explain: The tragic force tips the action from the climax into the fall.

questions.q: How does the classroom 'plot pyramid' usually differ from Freytag's own?
choices: It drops his three moments and often moves the climax toward the end
questions.explain: The school version simplifies Freytag and borrows his name for a different shape.

questions.q: A profile follows a CEO's climb, peak and long decline, with the peak halfway through. Whose shape is it closest to?
questions.explain: Freytag's pyramid rises to a central peak and falls for the second half.

ideas: A drama rises to its high point at the very center and spends its second half falling toward catastrophe.
Just before the end of a tragedy, a final flicker of hope should renew suspense.
A play is built from five parts joined by three decisive moments.
The first half shows the hero's will driving the action; the second shows the counter-forces driving the hero.
